chapter_title: Chương 239: 0241【Tiêu chuẩn của các ông lớn Internet】

segments.title: Chương 239: 0241【Tiêu chuẩn của các ông lớn Internet】
segments.content:
"CEO Chen, this is Mr. Huang Xinyuan, head of SP services at Push Sound."

"Hello."

"Hello, Boss Chen."

The man Xu Yuteng brought over was in his forties, slightly overweight, and wore glasses.

As for Push Sound, it was EMI Music's subsidiary in Mainland China. Over here, people usually didn't use its official name, referring to it simply as EMI Music.

Chen Guilang had his secretary make coffee, and after a few pleasantries, he asked, "EMI Music is doing its own SP services?"

Huang Xinyuan had a wry smile on his face. "They originally planned to set up an SP department and poached me for it, but then they suddenly decided not to. I've been left hanging for several months."

"What happened?" Chen Guilang was very curious.

Huang Xinyuan said, "There are many SP service providers in the country who bought the CRBT operation rights for a large number of songs from EMI and made an absolute fortune. The former president of Push Sound got jealous. He didn't want to just earn a small cut, so he planned to use the song copyrights in his hands to enter the SP business himself. I've always been the one running Hu Yanbing's song CRBTs. Since it was quite profitable, EMI poached me."

Chen Guilang's eyes lit up when he heard this. "You were the one running Hu Yanbing's CRBTs?"

Huang Xinyuan said, "I was the one who executed it. I used to work at TOM Online."

TOM Online was a powerhouse in CRBTs at the time, and its vice president, Xie Guoming, was a figure who directly influenced the landscape of Chinese music.

In a few years, Xie Guoming would become the vice president of Sina and the head of Sina Music.

Soon after, Xie Guoming would resign to found Haiyang Music, planning to spend a huge sum of money to buy up the rights to a massive catalog of songs. But his idea was too radical, and no one was willing to invest at the time.

So, he conned a real estate developer who knew nothing about music. The developer invested and obtained 100% of the equity in Haiyang Music. To circumvent the unlimited liability of a sole proprietorship, the developer had Xie Guoming hold 37.5% of the equity on his behalf. This nominal shareholding also included the option pool.

The developer was thoroughly duped. Faced with huge losses, he got scared and quickly sold his shares, tearfully earning 70 million in one year—from financing appreciation.

When the developer exited, Xie Guoming concealed four important agreements.

In reality, the developer could have made 700 million!

Of course, making 700 million was extremely difficult, as it was impossible to cash out. He would have had to continue holding the shares.

And Xie Guoming, using the funds obtained through continuous financing, bought the digital rights to 50% of the songs from all Chinese record companies at the time, just before the government stepped in to regulate music copyrights.

Then, he was absorbed by Tencent, becoming the Co-Vice President of Tencent Music.

When news of Tencent Music's US IPO broke, the real estate developer immediately came knocking, suing Xie Guoming for commercial fraud. To ensure a smooth IPO, Tencent Music quickly fired Xie Guoming and paid to buy out his shares. At the same time, they also compensated the developer to settle the matter.

This was how QQ Music conquered the market.

Xie Guoming's strategy of buying up digital rights at bargain prices beforehand was exactly what Chen Guilang planned to do in the future. Even if he just resold them later, he could make a hefty profit, on the order of billions of yuan.

Chen Guilang asked curiously, "How did EMI Music get into such a mess? They poached you to handle SP, and then suddenly dropped the business."

Huang Xinyuan explained in detail, "In the past, foreign companies were not allowed to independently handle audio-visual publishing in China. So, for EMI Music to establish a presence in Mainland China, it had to form a joint venture with a Chinese company. At that time, EMI Music partnered with Yifeng Music, and Yifeng Music, in turn, was working with Shanghai Culture & Broadcasting. But then China joined the WTO, didn't it?"

"So policy restrictions were relaxed?" Chen Guilang asked.

Huang Xinyuan nodded. "After joining the WTO, restrictions on foreign investment had to be gradually lifted. Although foreign companies still can't handle audio-visual publishing in the mainland, they can now own audio-visual distribution rights."

Thus, EMI Music headquarters invested a huge sum to turn Push Sound into a wholly-owned subsidiary. The publisher was still Shanghai Culture & Broadcasting, but Push Sound now held the distribution rights from them.

It was equivalent to EMI Music just giving Shanghai Culture & Broadcasting a cut, while being able to call the shots on everything else.

Over the past year, EMI's Asia President, Zheng Donghan, has been overhauling the management, replacing old hands with new ones. Most of the mid-to-high-level personnel being purged were from the former Yifeng Music, and some Taiwanese personnel were also let go.

The SP business that the previous president had decided to pursue was indefinitely shelved because of all this and could no longer proceed.

"You didn't sign a long-term contract with EMI too, did you?" Chen Guilang asked.

Huang Xinyuan laughed. "How could I? I'm not a musician. I didn't even sign a non-compete agreement. But having jumped ship from TOM Online, it's difficult for me to go back. And other SP service providers aren't exactly short on people like me. I heard CEO Chen also wants to get into the SP business, so I came to offer my services."

Chen Guilang said, "I'd like to ask you for the secret to success in the SP business."

"There's no secret. It all depends on your connections with China Mobile and China Unicom," Huang Xinyuan said. "You have to treat them to meals, get chummy with their business managers. Then you give them hidden kickbacks to get things settled. If you run into someone with special proclivities, you even have to take them to certain establishments for entertainment. Of course, for songs that are already extremely popular, you can still get by without doing all this."

Chen Guilang chuckled. "This industry is pretty shady."

Huang Xinyuan said, "It looks like this industry is very profitable, but after deducting all the kickbacks and the cuts for the songwriters and singers, the SP service provider only gets 15-20% of the CRBT revenue. And you only get 20% when the song is already a huge hit. Also, advertising on TV costs money, and that money comes out of the SP service provider's pocket."

Damn, I was careless. It seems the profit isn't that great after all.

"That does seem a bit low," Chen Guilang said.

Huang Xinyuan said, "It would be fine if that were all, but the biggest headache is piracy and infringement. Take *Jixiang Sanbao* for example. Only one company has the CRBT operation rights, but there are over a hundred companies making pirated CRBTs. These infringing companies even include Sohu and Huayou Shiji!"

Sohu needs no introduction.

Huayou Shiji had already gone public on the strength of its CRBT business.

Even these giants were infringing so blatantly.

One could only say that *Jixiang Sanbao* was too popular, making countless companies green with envy.

*The Wind Rises* being infringed upon only by Fenbei Wang was already considered very lucky.

With a case like *Jixiang Sanbao*, infringed upon by over a hundred companies, even the lawyers would get a headache just looking at it.

Huang Xinyuan then shared many other secrets of the CRBT industry, all to showcase his connections and abilities. This business relied on connections. For the same song, if you offended a provincial head at China Mobile, they could directly refuse to put it up!

Huang Xinyuan reminded him, "Some time ago, CEO Chen, you were making a fuss about suing a China Mobile branch, forcing Mobile to hand over download data to sue Fenbei Wang. You can't do that kind of thing again. If you offend China Mobile, you won't be able to run your SP business at all."

"In that case, I really was too much of an amateur," Chen Guilang humbly accepted the advice.

No wonder China Mobile and China Unicom acted as accomplices in infringement, yet no company dared to sue them. Only an amateur like Chen Guilang would foolishly make a fuss about suing.

Fortunately, they had already reached a settlement.

Chen Guilang also explained his own plans: to organize an original song competition through Xiaonei Wang and Hainei Wang, in collaboration with Xiami Music.
